title: Why Mosquitoes Bite You and Not Your Friends
description: Animal Secrets #30. Mosquitoes are picking you on purpose. We count down five reasons, from your breath and your red-glowing skin to Subject 33, who was 100 times tastier than others, and a new study of 119 people where not one person was the favorite of all three mosquito species. Are you the one who always gets bitten? Tell me in the comments. Part of the Wild Sketchbook.

scenes.say: Five friends, one barbecue, and only you go home with ten itchy bites.

scenes.label: Not bad luck
scenes.say: That's not bad luck. Mosquitoes are choosing you on purpose, and scientists can now explain how.
Okay, so today we count down five reasons a mosquito picks you out of a crowd.

scenes.label: Saved for #1
scenes.say: And stay for number one. It's a study that went around again this week, and it flips the whole idea of a mosquito magnet.

scenes.label: Only females bite
scenes.say: First, a quick thing most people don't know. The mosquito biting you is always a she.
The CDC says only female mosquitoes drink blood. They need it to make their eggs. Males just sip nectar and fruit juice.

scenes.label: Malaria carrier
scenes.say: And that tiny habit is deadly. Some female Anopheles mosquitoes carry malaria.

scenes.label: 610,000 deaths
scenes.say: The World Health Organization estimates malaria killed about 610,000 people in 2024 alone. Most were young children in Africa.
So knowing who mosquitoes choose, and why, isn't just about itchy ankles. It's life and death.
Every reason on this list is real, tested in a lab, with real numbers. And each one is a little stranger than the last.

scenes.label: Your breath
scenes.say: Number five. Your breath.
Every time you breathe out, you send carbon dioxide into the air. You can't smell it. A mosquito can.

scenes.label: Up to 15 meters
scenes.say: Their feathery antennae pick it up. A big scientific review says they can sense our breath from ten, even fifteen meters away.
That's like noticing someone breathing from the other side of a basketball court.
And the more you breathe out, the brighter you shine on their radar.

scenes.label: The hut test
scenes.say: Here's proof. In the Gambia, researchers had pregnant and non-pregnant women sleep in identical huts under bed nets.

scenes.label: Twice as many
scenes.say: Every morning they counted the mosquitoes. The pregnant women attracted about twice as many.
Why? Late in pregnancy, those women breathed out about 21 percent more air. And their bellies were about 0.7 degrees warmer.
More breath, more heat. To a mosquito, that's a giant flashing sign that says dinner.
The pregnant women also left the hut at night about twice as often. Every trip outside was another chance to get noticed.
So if you're bigger, breathing hard, or just finished a run, you're louder on their radar. But breath only gets them close.

scenes.label: Heat and color
scenes.say: Number four. Your heat, and your color.
Your skin sits at about 34 degrees Celsius. That warmth glows as infrared light, which you can't see.

scenes.label: About 70 cm
scenes.say: In 2024, scientists showed in the journal Nature that the dengue mosquito can sense that glow from about 70 to 80 centimeters away.
That's roughly an arm's length. So once one gets that close, your body heat is pulling it in like a tractor beam.

scenes.label: Favorite color?
scenes.say: But here's the twist. Mosquitoes also hunt with their eyes, and they have a favorite color.

scenes.label: 1.3 million flights
scenes.say: At the University of Washington, a team tracked more than 1.3 million mosquito flight paths in a wind tunnel.
Before they smelled breath, the mosquitoes ignored colored dots. After a puff of carbon dioxide, everything changed.

scenes.label: Red, not green
scenes.say: Suddenly they flew straight at red, orange, black and cyan. Green, blue, purple and white? Mostly ignored.
And this part is wild. Every human skin, whatever its shade, gives off a strong red-orange signal to a mosquito's eyes.
When a researcher covered their hand with a green glove, the mosquitoes lost interest. So, quick question. What color are you wearing right now?

scenes.label: The drink
scenes.say: Number three. That drink in your hand.

scenes.label: Beer vs water
scenes.say: In a 2010 study, scientists tested 25 volunteers before and after drinking beer, and 18 more who drank only water.
They released thousands of malaria mosquitoes into a Y-shaped tube and let them choose which body smell to fly toward.
Think of it like a mosquito taste test, with your smell as the menu. Water changed nothing. But after beer, the volunteers' body odor made more mosquitoes take off and fly toward them.

scenes.label: Still a mystery
scenes.say: Here's the strange part. It wasn't extra breath, and it wasn't body heat. Both were measured, and neither explained it.
So something in beer drinkers' scent changes, and nobody knows exactly what. The scientists even called beer a risk factor for malaria.

scenes.label: Myth check
scenes.say: Okay, quick myth check, since everyone asks. What about your blood type?
A review in the journal Cell said the evidence for blood type or certain foods is either lacking or contradictory. So don't blame your blood.
The real answer is hiding somewhere much weirder. On your skin.

scenes.label: Mosquito magnet
scenes.say: Number two. The mosquito magnet.

scenes.label: 64 volunteers
scenes.say: At Rockefeller University in New York, 64 volunteers wore nylon stockings on their arms for six hours.
Then scientists ran a tournament nobody wants to win. Two stockings at a time, mosquitoes picking a side.

scenes.label: 3 years
scenes.say: Round after round. Pair after pair. For more than three years.
And here's the clever part. The testers didn't know whose stocking was whose. So nobody could cheat.
And one person crushed everyone. Volunteer number 33.

scenes.label: 100x tastier
scenes.say: Subject 33 was four times more attractive than the next person, and more than 100 times more attractive than the least attractive.
The lead scientist said it was obvious within a few seconds. The mosquitoes just swarmed toward that stocking.

scenes.label: Skin acids
scenes.say: So what made Subject 33 so delicious? Fatty acids called carboxylic acids, made in the oily layer on your skin.
The biggest magnets had much more of them. And it didn't fade. If you were a magnet, you stayed a magnet, for years.
Diet, soap, a new routine. None of it seemed to change the ranking. One scientist joked it's good news or bad news, depending on who you are.
So that's it, right? Some people are just mosquito magnets for life. Well, a newer study says, not quite.

scenes.label: Not every type
scenes.say: Number one. You're not every mosquito's type.

scenes.label: Dengue surge
scenes.say: And this is why it's back in the news. Florida has had a dengue surge, with 425 local cases reported this year by mid-October.
That's compared with 62 in all of 2025. So scientists in Miami asked a sharper question.

scenes.label: 119 volunteers
scenes.say: At Florida International University, 119 volunteers put one forearm into a small box at the end of a tube.
A mesh screen kept them safe. The mosquitoes could smell the arm, but not bite it.

scenes.label: Day biter
scenes.say: Then they tested three different mosquitoes. First, Aedes aegypti, the daytime dengue mosquito.

scenes.label: Tiger mosquito
scenes.say: Second, the Asian tiger mosquito, with its black and white striped legs.

scenes.label: Night biter
scenes.say: And third, the southern house mosquito. It bites at night and can spread West Nile virus.
Now, if mosquito magnets were real for every species, the same people would win every round. Right?

scenes.label: Not one person
scenes.say: They didn't. Not one of the 119 people was a top favorite of all three mosquitoes.
The dengue mosquito liked people with less smell, and no added perfume. It even preferred men, just slightly, about 92 to 87 percent.
The tiger mosquito wanted the opposite. People whose skin gave off more ketones and plant-like smells.

scenes.label: Skin bacteria
scenes.say: And the night mosquito seemed to read your skin bacteria. Some bacteria were a green light. Others seemed to push it away.
Your skin gives off more than a thousand different smell chemicals, and lots of them are made by those tiny bacteria.
The scientists say each mosquito species learned to decode your personal smell signature in its own way.
To be fair, it's a lab study. It measured attraction, not real bites. And there's no special repellent from it yet.
So the best protection is still the boring stuff. Repellent, long sleeves, bed nets, and no standing water near your home.

scenes.label: Day vs night
scenes.say: But think about what it means. Your friend who never gets bitten at lunch might be the main course at midnight.
So that's why it's always you. Your breath, your heat, your drink, your skin acids, and the exact mosquito that's hungry.
Now tell me in the comments. Are you the one who always gets bitten? And is it worse in the day, or at night?

short.title: Subject 33 Was 100x Tastier to Mosquitoes
short.description: In a 3-year Rockefeller University tournament, Subject 33's skin scent beat every other volunteer, over 100 times more attractive than the least attractive (De Obaldia et al., Cell 2022). Full countdown of why mosquitoes bite you on my channel.

scenes.say: Why did mosquitoes love one person 100 times more than others? Could it be you?
Scientists in New York had 64 people wear nylon stockings on their arms for six hours.
Then mosquitoes picked between two stockings at a time. A tournament that ran for more than three years.
One person won almost every round. Volunteer number 33. The mosquitoes swarmed within seconds, and the least attractive people barely got a look.
The reason? Way more fatty acids on the skin. Not their soap. Not their diet.
And it didn't change for years. Once a mosquito magnet, always a mosquito magnet.
So if you always get bitten, you might be the next Subject 33. Because in that lab, mosquitoes loved one person 100 times more than others.
